top_comments.text:
Eating lots of fat was great for me health wise, but it stalled me out for years. I had awesome health, but i stayed fat - 14 + stone for a woman 5ft6in. High protein, high fat.
The only thing that worked for me to lose fat again - after the initial 70lb fat loss in my first year of carnivore (carnivore nearly 7 years now - in december) was to fast. 
Fasting is the only thing that lowers my insulin levels enough to make my body burn its own fat.
Even dropping dairy didn't work. I needed to fast. 

Fasting 5 days broke the stall. So i continue to fast. Sometimes 5 days, 2 weeks here and there.. I eat a whole carnivore diet - including dairy, and then fast for as long as i like - taking only salt and vitamins upon waking during these prolonged fasts. The fat just melts away - very quickly. And for me, there's no cons! No food noise, no weakness, great sleep, lots of focus and energy - workouts at the gym are 🔥🔥🔥.. its just all positive. And then when i break my fast, I just eat eggs, broth and a light meat - depending on the length of the fast. Minimum is 5 days.  

Fasting is the only way imo 🤷🏾‍♀️

Fasting and carnivore is 🔥🔥🔥

   I am curious about your  protein advice, however. At age 77, 5' 8.5", carnivore, and in a long stall at current weight 275 (I gained 20 lbs recently after including dairy again), my LBM isn't very high. Using an online formula to determine it, I came up with 65.5, but it's hard to believe that 65 grams of protein would be enough for me, and especially at my age, when we need more protein in general!
   I did recently double that number to 120g, however, based on other considerations, and I split it equally between 2 meals. And finally, for probably the first time in my life, I know what true satiety and satisfaction feel like! I even started losing weight again!
    And I've even discovered that if I eat this amount early in the day, starting with breakfast around 8 to 9 am, I am still satisfied and desire nothing else even late into the night, if I don't fall asleep first. My only issue with it, however, is not eating enough fat to at least keep my stools comfortably soft. So I will definitely start increasing my butter and olive oil again. Thanks for that reminder. But do you agree that for the over 70 set, more protein is probably needed than in your formula?
   Btw, I was aiming for the amount of protein that I've heard is the perfect amount for my body to satisfy it. That when we reach that ideal number, I body stops hungering for anything more, whereas when we have less than that amount, we continue to hunger for something, usually carbs. 
  And now that I know 120g at least reaches that number, I'm resting to see if it actually exceeds it by slowly lowering my daily intake until I start feeling hungry again later in the day. Then I'll know my intake needs to be higher than that.

top_comments.text:
The "they just died earlier" argument doesn't hold up against consecutive year-on-year data.

Here's why:•Year-on-year increases over THE MOST REVENT 5 years can't be explained by "living slightly longer" — If it were just about increased life expectancy, you'd see a one-off jump when old data meets new methodology, not a consistent upward trend every single year.

Age-standardised rates already control for age structure — Epidemiological data usually reports age-adjusted incidence precisely to remove the confounding effect of an ageing population.

Incidence (new cases) vs survival — Higher survival from other causes would increase prevalence, but the argument falls apart when you're looking at new diagnoses rising every year across multiple demographics.

The trend is consistent across Western populations — If it were purely a historical artefact, you'd see plateauing once detection normalised. Instead, the trend continues.

5 consecutive years of rising rates = a pattern, not a statistical artefact — You can't explain away a sustained multi-year trend with better diagnostics or marginal life expectancy gains.

Bottom line: The "died before they could get it" argument might work as a partial explanation for some historical undercounting, but it completely fails to explain persistent, year-on-year increases in modern incidence data.
